overview: Coast Salish is a collective name for many independent Indigenous Nations around the Salish Sea, including coastal British Columbia and Washington. Their related languages, trade and family connections never made them one empire. The map’s broad outline and 1492 to 1500 interval are approximate coverage; each example below names its community, and the people continue today.

periods.title: Ancient villages and managed harvests
periods.summary: Archaeology documents long-established fishing communities and varied harvesting strategies around Burrard Inlet.

periods.title: Colonial settlement and land loss
periods.summary: Treaties, dispossession and attacks on communal life reshaped different communities in different ways.

periods.title: Communities organize
periods.summary: Squamish bands joined their resources and governance in 1923; their people’s history was already ancient.

periods.title: Rights, teaching and stewardship
periods.summary: Treaty fishing rights and cooperative fisheries management became central to regional political life.

items.text: Suquamish winter villages stood along waterways, with cedar-plank houses shared by multiple families. During spring, summer and early fall, relatives traveled by canoe to fishing, hunting and gathering camps. A household’s year followed the places where food and useful materials became available.

Ancient salmon backbones can preserve clues invisible to the eye. A 2021 study used DNA to identify the sex of fish from four ancestral Coast Salish settlements in Burrard Inlet. Two sites, Tum-tumay-wheuton and DhRr 22, contained significantly more male chum salmon; the other two did not show that pattern.

The researchers interpret those remains as evidence of selective fishing before European colonization. Male chum are larger, and leaving more females can support future spawning. They also acknowledge that the fishers’ exact motives cannot be recovered from bones alone. Local choices mattered, even between neighboring settlements.

Hul’q’umi’num’ and WSÁNEĆ sea gardens use low stone walls to hold sediment and form terraces where shellfish thrive. Maintaining them includes turning the beach sediment and removing excess sea lettuce. This is gardening with tides: in winter, the lowest water can send the work crew out in the middle of the night.

Parks Canada’s report for 2018 to 2023 records more than 320 metres of sea-garden walls rebuilt and over 11,700 square metres of beach habitat maintained with Indigenous partners. Elders, community members and volunteers put inherited knowledge into practice while restoring a local food supply.

sections.title: Woolly dogs, skilled hands and family learning

items.text: Some Coast Salish families raised small woolly dogs for their thick hair, which could be spun into textiles. A tear in a blanket now at the Burke Museum exposed unusual yarn; testing confirmed dog hair. The blanket, catalogued 2.5E1965, preserves remarkable skill, although its maker’s name was not recorded.

A spindle whorl is a disk fitted around a rod. Its weight helps a spinner control the twist and thickness of yarn; the carved face points toward the person spinning. In the Burke exhibition, wood, stone and bone versions show how a small, carefully balanced tool can do a large amount of work.

The same exhibition describes cleaning wool with diatomaceous earth, a powder sprinkled into the fibers. Beating the wool over a cedar mat lets the powder fall through, carrying dirt and oil away. Long before a blanket could keep someone warm, its fibers needed a very thorough clean.

A modern Tulalip Lushootseed lesson prints “haʔɬ dadatu təkʷtəkʷəlus”, translated “Good morning owl.” It is a real phrase from the community’s language department, written in its modern alphabet. Lushootseed is one of the region’s languages; this friendly owl greeting is not presented as a sentence shared by every Coast Salish Nation.

In 2019, Tulalip News reported two full Lushootseed classes at Marysville Pilchuck High School. Lessons used everyday subjects such as weather, feelings and daily routines, alongside archived recordings of elders. Students could hear community speakers directly while learning words to use beyond the classroom.

At the 1855 Treaty of Point Elliott, Suquamish leaders ceded extensive lands while reserving a homeland and fishing, hunting and gathering rights. The Tribe’s history describes difficult translation through Chinook Jargon into local languages. Those hurried negotiations had consequences that generations later still had to challenge in court.

The destruction of Old Man House in 1870 struck at Suquamish communal life. Families continued living around the site before being forced onto individual allotments in 1904. Requirements that children attend boarding schools further separated young people from family teaching and language.

On July 23, 1923, sixteen Squamish bands amalgamated into the modern Squamish Nation. They pooled property, interests and accounts held in trust to strengthen collective government. This was a deliberate response to colonial interference and unequal treatment, not the beginning of Squamish identity.

The 1974 Boldt decision affirmed treaty tribes’ right to half the harvestable salmon at their usual and accustomed fishing places and established them as co-managers with Washington State. The ruling followed a long struggle over promises made in nineteenth-century treaties.

Musqueam community member Jordan Wilson recalls keeping vigil at the ancient village of c̓əsnaʔəm in 2012. The vigil lasted over 200 days as people worked to protect the site. He also recalls learning respect, patience and care for family while fishing with his grandfather.

ending.text: There was no single Coast Salish state to fall in 1500. Colonial land loss, coercive schooling and restrictions on community life caused profound harm, but the Nations survive as distinct peoples and governments. Language teaching, weaving, fisheries management and protection of ancestral places remain living responsibilities.
